\subsection{Main comparison}
\resulttable{CIC17_main_b010_paper.tex}{CIC-IDS2017, label budget 10\%, delay 1 window.}{tab:cic17}
\resulttable{IDS18_main_b010_paper.tex}{CSE-CIC-IDS2018, label budget 10\%, delay 1 window.}{tab:ids18}
\resulttable{UNSW_main_b010_paper.tex}{UNSW-NB15 (four classes held out of training), label budget 10\%.}{tab:unsw}

\textbf{CIC-IDS2017} (\cref{tab:cic17}). \nova{} has the highest OW-F1 (0.768) and AUT (0.858). The closest
baseline, CBRS replay (0.756, 0.838; Wilcoxon $p < 0.001$), detects slightly more attacks (detection F1 0.861
against 0.854) but at a 4.5\% false-positive rate against 2.8\%: \nova{} sends 38\% fewer benign flows to the
analyst. All other methods are at least 12 points lower.

\textbf{CSE-CIC-IDS2018} (\cref{tab:ids18}). \nova{} and CBRS replay tie on OW-F1 (0.722) and AUT (0.869);
\nova{} wins 51 of 70 windows ($p = 0.003$) but trails over the last 24. It has the higher detection F1 (0.815
against 0.788), a 3.1\% against 4.8\% false-positive rate, and five times less forgetting (0.007 against 0.034).

\textbf{UNSW-NB15} (\cref{tab:unsw}, \cref{fig:time-unsw}). Most adaptive methods end \emph{below} the static
model (0.499); CBRS replay reaches 0.327. They learn Exploits and Fuzzers, but every later flow of these classes is
rejected as \unk{}: the thresholds were calibrated on January traffic, and February flows of the same classes lie
outside them. \nova{} recalibrates learned classes on its calibration store and reaches 0.509 OW-F1 and 0.595
AUT, ahead of the static model ($p = 0.03$), with the highest detection F1 (0.860) and lowest false-positive rate
(6.6\% against 7.6--19.0\%). Removing the calibration store (a check run after the main results, method
unchanged) drops \nova{} to 0.418 and zero F1 on Exploits and Fuzzers, confirming the mechanism.

INSOMNIA's self-training has the highest false-positive rate on both CIC datasets (12.4\%, 25.7\%):
pseudo-label errors on unseen classes are fed back into training.

\subsection{Label budget}
With 1\% of each window labelled (\cref{tab:budget}), \nova{} leads by 9.0 points on CIC-IDS2017 and by 3.4
points on CSE-CIC-IDS2018 ($p = 0.002$), where the two methods tied at 10\%. On UNSW-NB15 it trails periodic
retraining (0.469 against 0.504). With 40 labels per window, periodic retraining never collects enough labels of
the held-out classes to learn them, so it keeps rejecting them as \unk{}, which the metric credits in full, while
scoring 0 on Exploits and Fuzzers. \nova{} learns DoS and Reconnaissance, which overlap with Exploits in
UNSW-NB15, and loses that credit. It still halves the false-positive rate (9.7\% against $\geq$15.7\%).

\subsection{Ablation and detector}
\resulttable{CIC17_ablation_b010_paper.tex}{Ablation on CIC-IDS2017 (budget 10\%): \nova{} with one component removed.}{tab:ablation}

Every component raises OW-F1 (\cref{tab:ablation}; full \nova{} 0.768). The guard matters most ($-5.6$):
without it more updates are deployed, which flag more attacks (detection recall 0.836 against 0.799) but name the
right class less often. The query is next ($-4.2$; unknown AUROC 0.826 without it), followed by recency
weighting, the calibration store and the balanced memory ($-1.9$ to $-2.3$). Propagation adds least to OW-F1
($-1.2$) but lowers the false-positive rate (3.6\% without it). Replacing the class-conditional $k$-NN detector by
distance to the nearest class centroid lowers OW-F1 from 0.768 to 0.712 for \nova{} and from 0.311 to 0.178 for
the static model, which then labels almost every attack benign: one centroid cannot follow multi-modal benign
traffic.

\textbf{Neural classifier.} With an MLP instead of gradient boosting on CIC-IDS2017, \nova{} keeps the lowest
false-positive rate (3.3\% against 4.7\%), the higher detection F1 and an equal AUT, but its OW-F1 is lower than
CBRS replay's (0.622 against 0.711), mainly on two short-lived web attacks. We do not claim that its accuracy
advantage carries over to neural classifiers.
